title: Federated Learning With Explainable AI for Malicious Traffic Detection in IoT Networks
researchArea: Cybersecurity, Federated Learning, Explainable AI, IoT Intrusion Detection Systems
problem: Centralizing raw IoT network traffic data for deep learning-based intrusion detection raises serious privacy, bandwidth, and scalability concerns, while black-box deep learning models lack transparency and human-understandable justifications for security analysts.
motivation: The explosive growth of connected IoT devices increases vulnerability to large-scale attacks like Mirai botnets and DDoS. An effective intrusion detection system must preserve data privacy and locality through federated learning while offering transparent, instance-level explainability via post-hoc XAI to establish operational trust in security operation centers.
noveltyAndContributions: Proposed a unified FL-XAI framework combining a lightweight multi-layer perceptron deep neural network with SHAP and LIME for malicious traffic detection across distributed IoT networks.
Integrated KernelSHAP for global and instance-level feature attributions alongside LIME for local surrogate explanations to enhance alert transparency without compromising detection accuracy.
Rigorously evaluated the system on three recent, comprehensive IoT/IIoT benchmark datasets (Edge-IIoT, CIC-IoT2023, and TII-SSRC-23) under both IID and non-IID client partitioning scenarios.
Demonstrated near-centralized detection performance with less than 0.5 percent performance gap while maintaining low communication overhead and preserving client data locality.
methodology: Standardized data preprocessing including data cleaning, feature selection pruning zero-variance and highly correlated attributes, one-hot encoding for categorical variables, port binning, and Min-Max normalization scaling continuous features to range 0 to 1.
Cost-sensitive loss formulation using weighted cross-entropy and focal loss with SMOTE restricted to extreme minority classes to address severe dataset class imbalance.
Lightweight multi-layer perceptron neural network architecture with 2 hidden layers (128 and 64 neurons with ReLU activation and 20 percent dropout) trained using Adam optimizer.
Horizontal federated learning using Federated Averaging across 4 to 5 client nodes simulating IoT edge devices.
Post-hoc explainability module applying KernelSHAP with 100 benign background samples and LIME with 500 perturbations per instance for alert interpretation.
keyAssumptions: IoT edge nodes can train lightweight neural network models locally and share model updates with a central server without transmitting raw network traffic logs.
The central aggregator server possesses sufficient computational resources to execute SHAP and LIME post-hoc explanation modules on global model predictions.
Feature schemas and label taxonomies are standardized per dataset across federated clients in a horizontal federated learning setting.
datasets: Edge-IIoT (2022) dataset with 40 selected features across DoS/DDoS, Information Gathering, MITM, Injection, and Malware attack categories.
CIC-IoT2023 dataset with 45 selected features spanning 33 attack types organized into 7 families (DDoS, DoS, Reconnaissance, Mirai, Spoofing, Web, BruteForce).
TII-SSRC-23 (2023) dataset with 52 selected features aggregated into 5 broad attack categories across industrial and smart IoT devices.
partition: 80:20 train and test split per dataset.
Partitioned across 4 to 5 federated clients simulating device-type or attack-family non-IID skewed distributions as well as IID baseline configurations.
numClients: 5 clients for Edge-IIoT partitioned by device type
4 clients for CIC-IoT2023 partitioned by attack family
5 clients for TII-SSRC-23 partitioned by device category
experimentalSetup: Central server: Intel Core i7 CPU (8 cores), 16 GB RAM; Google Colaboratory GPU (Tesla K80, 12 GB RAM) for large workloads.
Software: Python, TensorFlow 2.x/Keras, custom FedAvg loop, SHAP library (v0.41), LIME package, scikit-learn, Pandas, NumPy.
Hyperparameters: Adam optimizer with initial learning rate 0.001, batch size 64, 1 to 2 local epochs per round, early stopping with patience of 5 rounds.
Loss function: Cost-sensitive weighted cross-entropy and focal loss (focusing parameter gamma=2, balance parameter beta).
baselines: Centralized DNN model trained on all dataset samples
Ferrag et al. centralized XGBoost on Edge-IIoT
DIoT (Nguyen et al.) federated anomaly detection
DeepFed (Li et al.) federated deep learning for industrial IoT
Centralized models by Hasan et al., Alshehri et al., and Saadouni et al. (Edge-IIoT)
Centralized Transformer (Tseng et al.), Random Forest (Elkhadir and Begdouri), and LSTM (Jony and Arnob) (CIC-IoT2023)
Centralized XGBoost (Herzalla et al.) and GAN-based method (Rani et al.) (TII-SSRC-23)
xaiEvaluation: Evaluated feature attributions using mean absolute SHAP values normalized by maximum to generate global rankings, paired with instance-level LIME local contribution plots on 10 top features across held-out test samples to verify consistency between global model behavior and local alert rationales.
results: The FL-XAI model achieved binary classification accuracies of 99.3% (Edge-IIoT), 99.5% (CIC-IoT2023), and 99.0% (TII-SSRC-23), with corresponding multi-class accuracies of 97.2%, 98.0%, and 96.5%. The performance gap between federated and centralized models was negligible (<0.5% F1-score difference). SHAP and LIME provided consistent, domain-aligned feature attributions (e.g., packet rates for DDoS, protocol function codes for industrial IoT) without sacrificing detection quality.
failureConditions: Minor inter-class confusion observed in multi-class Edge-IIoT between DoS/DDoS and Injection attacks due to overlapping traffic flow characteristics.
Stealthy Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attacks occasionally misclassified as benign or injection due to subtle TCP and ARP behavior changes.
LIME local explanations occasionally missed port-related behaviors in MITM traffic, requiring feature discretization.
costEvaluation: Total communication overhead per client over 50 rounds was below 30 MB due to lightweight MLP parameters (13.8k to 15.3k float32 weights). Inference memory usage stayed under a few megabytes. SHAP computations took approximately 0.2 seconds per instance and LIME approximately 0.5 seconds on CPU, suitable for post-alert security analyst interpretation.

limitations.text: Computing SHAP and LIME explanations incurs computational latency on CPU (0.2s and 0.5s per instance), making real-time inline XAI generation per packet challenging.
Post-hoc explanations reflect model behavior but do not directly influence or correct classification decisions during runtime.
Evaluations relied on standard FedAvg which may experience performance degradation under extreme non-IID client distributions without proximal or Byzantine-robust mechanisms.

futureWork: Develop communication-efficient federated learning strategies and adaptive client selection algorithms.
Implement client-level personalization to better accommodate extreme non-IID IoT traffic environments.
Integrate real-time feedback loops from security analysts to dynamically refine detection models.
Explore advanced Byzantine-robust aggregation methods against malicious client updates.
relevance: Highly relevant for privacy-preserving IoT cybersecurity, edge-cloud intrusion detection, trustworthy explainable AI, and multi-dataset federated learning benchmarks.
newIdeas: Combining FedAvg horizontal federated learning with post-hoc KernelSHAP and LIME explanation modules for multi-dataset IoT intrusion detection.
Pairing normalized global SHAP rankings with instance-level LIME local contribution bars over identical top-10 feature subsets to cross-verify alert explanation consistency.
